rules.title: Charge
rules.plain: Charge is an amount of electricity. One coulomb is about 6.24 × 10<sup>18</sup> electrons' worth.

rules.title: Current
rules.plain: Current is how much charge passes a point each second. One ampere is one coulomb per second.

rules.title: Voltage
rules.plain: Voltage is energy per coulomb: what each coulomb gains in the supply and gives up in the parts.

rules.title: Capacitance
rules.plain: A capacitor holds charge in proportion to the voltage across it. Capacitance is the ratio: coulombs per volt.
rules.example: 1000 µF at 5 V: Q = C × V = 0.001 × 5 = 0.005 C (5 millicoulombs).

rules.title: Ohm's law
rules.plain: For a resistor, voltage and current stay in proportion, and the ratio R doesn't change. That ratio is what an ohm measures: volts per amp. Georg Ohm measured it in 1827; it's an observation about materials, not a definition you can prove.
rules.example: The triangle in the logo is a memory aid: cover the letter you want. V = I × R, I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I. That's one law rearranged by algebra, not three laws.

rules.title: The junction rule (KCL)
rules.plain: At any junction, the current flowing in equals the current flowing out. Charge is never created or destroyed, and it can't pile up in a wire. (Kirchhoff's current law.)

rules.title: The loop rule (KVL)
rules.short: Σ rises = Σ drops, around any loop
rules.plain: Go around any closed loop and the voltage the supply gives equals the voltage the parts use. A coulomb that goes all the way round ends where it started, with the energy it started with. (Kirchhoff's voltage law.)

rules.title: The LED resistor
rules.plain: The resistor takes whatever voltage the LED doesn't, and Ohm's law turns that into a resistance.
rules.given: A supply Vs, a resistor R and an LED in one loop; the LED holds its forward voltage Vf.
proof: The resistor carries the LED's current, I
rules.example: Level 1: (5 − 2.0) ÷ 0.010 = 300 Ω. The next standard value up is 330 Ω, which gives 9.1 mA.

rules.title: Series circuits
rules.short: same I everywhere; the V's add up
rules.plain: In a single loop there's nowhere else for the current to go, so every part carries the same current, and the drops share out the supply.
rules.given: Parts connected end to end in one loop, with no branches.
proof: At each joint between two parts, current in = current out
The joints have no third wire, so the current leaving one part is the current entering the next
Every part carries the same current I
With n LEDs in series: R = (V<sub>s</sub> − n·V<sub>f</sub>) ÷ I
rules.example: Level 2: two green LEDs at 2.08 V each and 150 Ω: (5 − 4.16) ÷ 150 = 5.6 mA, the same through all three parts.

rules.title: Power in a resistor
rules.plain: Power is energy per second (1 watt = 1 joule per second). A resistor turns it into heat, which is why resistors have a watt rating.
rules.given: A resistor R with voltage V across it and current I through it.
proof: P = I × R × I = I² × R  ∎
rules.example: Level 1's 330 Ω at 9.1 mA: 0.0091² × 330 = 27 mW, far inside a ¼ W resistor.

rules.title: Ohms × farads = seconds
rules.plain: Resistance times capacitance comes out in seconds, whatever the values. The units prove it.
proof: 1 kΩ × 1000 µF = 10<sup>3</sup> Ω × 10<sup>−3</sup> F = 1 Ω·F = 1 s
rules.example: This proves the units, not yet why R × C is the capacitor's clock. That's the next two theorems.

rules.title: The fraction rule
rules.plain: A capacitor draining through a resistor loses the same fraction of its voltage in every equal slice of time. It's always the same fraction; the amount shrinks as the voltage does.
rules.given: A capacitor C at voltage V, draining through a resistor R; Δt is a slice of time short enough that V barely changes during it.
proof: The resistor has the capacitor's voltage V across it
The current through it is I = V ÷ R
In the slice Δt, the charge that leaves is ΔQ = I × Δt
Losing ΔQ lowers the voltage by ΔV = ΔQ ÷ C
ΔV = (V ÷ R) × Δt ÷ C = V × Δt ÷ (R × C)
rules.example: With R × C = 1 s, every 10 ms slice takes away 1% of whatever voltage is left.

rules.title: R × C is the capacitor's clock
rules.short: empty at the starting rate in R × C; 37% left after it
rules.plain: If it kept draining at its starting rate, the capacitor would be empty after exactly R × C. It doesn't keep that rate, because each slice takes a fraction of what's left, so after R × C about 37% remains.
rules.given: The draining capacitor of @fraction, starting at V₀.
proof: At the start it loses V₀ × Δt ÷ (RC) per slice: V₀ ÷ (RC) per second
At that constant rate, all of V₀ would be gone after t = RC
V₀ ÷ (RC) × t = V₀ ⇒ t = RC (the tangent line in the figure)
Cut RC into n equal slices. Each keeps (1 − 1/n) of the voltage before it
After all n slices: V = V₀ × (1 − 1/n)<sup>n</sup>
The limit that defines e (compound interest, run backwards)
After R × C, 36.8% of V₀ remains: it has drained about ⅔  ∎
In general, after time t the fraction left is e<sup>−t/RC</sup>; after 5 RC it's under 1%
The same limit with t instead of RC; 0.368<sup>5</sup> ≈ 0.007
rules.example: Level 6's glow fades to a fifth when e<sup>−t/RC</sup> = ⅕, at t = RC × ln 5 ≈ 1.6 RC. That's the 1.6 you measured.

rules.title: Filling to a threshold
rules.short: reaches ⅔ of the supply after RC × ln 3 ≈ 1.1 RC
rules.plain: Charging is draining in a mirror: the capacitor closes the GAP to the supply by the same fraction per slice, so the gap shrinks like the clock theorem says.
rules.given: A capacitor charging from 0 V toward the supply Vs through R, and a switch point at ⅔ Vs (the 555's pin 6).
proof: The resistor has the gap (Vs − V) across it, so the gap shrinks by Δt ÷ (RC) of itself per slice
@fraction, with the gap in place of V
After time t the gap is Vs × e<sup>−t/RC</sup>
At ⅔ Vs the gap is ⅓ Vs, so e<sup>−t/RC</sup> = ⅓
Take the natural log of both sides
rules.example: Level 9: 100 kΩ × 10 µF × 1.0986 = 1.10 s, what the simulator measured.

rules.title: The blink formula
rules.plain: The capacitor bounces between ⅓ and ⅔ of the supply. Each trip halves a gap, and halving a gap takes RC × ln 2.
rules.given: The level-10 astable: C fills through R1 + R2 and drains through R2 into pin 7, switching at ⅓ and ⅔ of Vs.
proof: Rising from ⅓ to ⅔ Vs, the gap to Vs goes from ⅔ Vs to ⅓ Vs: it halves
Halving a gap through R1 + R2 takes (R1 + R2) × C × ln 2
Falling from ⅔ to ⅓ Vs through R2, the voltage halves
rules.example: Level 10: 0.693 × (10k + 136k) × 10 µF = 1.01 s per blink, about 1 Hz.

rules.title: The voltage divider
rules.plain: Two resistances in series share the supply in proportion to their size; the joint sits at the bottom one's share.
rules.given: R1 and R2 in series across Vin (R2 at the bottom, to ground), and nothing drawing current from the joint.
proof: The same current I flows through R1 and R2
Vin = I × R1 + I × R2 = I × (R1 + R2)
The joint's voltage is the drop across R2: Vout = I × R2
rules.example: Level 12's pot at 34%: the track below the wiper is 6.6 kΩ of 10 kΩ, so 5 × 6.6 ÷ 10 = 3.3 V.
